newsitem.title: UK: IPE natgas changes meet mixed reaction from trade.
newsitem.headline: IPE natgas changes meet mixed reaction from trade.

text.p: The changes to the natural gas futures contract unveiled by the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) on Tuesday evening have drawn a mixed reaction from gas traders and futures brokers.

The IPE will introduce a number of changes on August 8. These include trading the Balance of the Month contract on the screen-based Energy Trading System (ETS); extending the trading hours from 10.00 hrs to 17.00 hrs with no midday closure; and increasing the minimum tick size from 0.005 pence to 0.01 penny a therm.

A new regulatory regime has also been approved. Trade associate members of the exchange can now be regulated by the IPE itself and will not need authorisation by the Securities and Futures Authority or the Securities and Investments Board.
And the exchange has announced it is considering establishing a market maker scheme to ensure quotes are available in all months listed at as narrow a range as possible.
"There's been a good reaction," said one futures broker. "It's making the whole thing more user friendly and in line with the market out there."
But he added that the introduction of trade in quarters as opposed to single months is needed to allow trade to take off.
"These are just small changes to help the system, they won't help to improve liquidity in themselves."
Another futures broker was less positive. "Will it make a difference? Well, the Balance of the Month contract might. The rest is of no interest," he said.
He added that the market maker scheme was of no benefit and his company would not be willing to participate.
"The thing that will make a difference is the introduction of a day ahead contract. Until they apply themselves to that, this is just tinkering," he said.
And he said that extending the contract to two years forward, allowing quarterly trade in the outer periods, will also be important.

One trader on the OTC market believes the IPE is moving in the wrong direction. "On the Balance of the Month, I think they're trying to compete too closely with the OTC market, and their costs are too great, so it probably won't be used," he said.

And he was not positive on the issue of trading quarters. "The value of the IPE is that you can split out the months," he said, and trade them individually even when the OTC market is only trading quarters and there are no readily available quotes for individual months.
He believes the contract is already becoming too closely associated with physical delivery.

This is especially true of the introduction of a Balance of the Month contract, he said, which at the time of purchase will have only a limited life before going to physical delivery and so will be hard to trade as a pure futures contract.

There are two main reasons why the exchange is not now trading actively, the trader said. First it is expensive compared with the OTC market, to which he believes it adds little value; and second, gas companies do not have enough personnel to monitor the screen as closely as they would need to if trade is really to take off.
"The IPE must make a decision if it is to be a futures contract or just set up as a broker," he added.
